vcb.etymoprose: Due to the extreme similarity to psmt@ṯawr- of the same meaning, it is likely this word was borrowed from one language into the other or from a common source. §Kroonen3§ assumes a Pre-Proto-Indo-European form _*þaur_ which at some point was raised to _*þeur_; he draws a comparison to ett@𐌈𐌄𐌖𐌓-=thevr- for the change in diphthong. While the dental fricative would have been rendered as a stop in all extant Indo-European languages, a secondary approximation through /st/ would explain pgmc@steuraz. §Matasović6§ mentions that sqi@ter may be a loan from Latin instead. It is unclear if the Balto-Slavic mobile accent originates from an original suffixal accent, which would contrast with Graeco-Carite, or if it is a later development.

A derivation from the root pie@@kʷel- is sometimes suggested; however, the delabialisation in Germano-Carite would be irregular. §Ringe0§ specifically labels the formation as Post-Proto-Indo-European. mga@coll “head, chief”, which is mentioned by §Mallory2§, is considered a loan from Latin by §de Vaan1§.
§Klein0§ reconstructs an additional _*h₁_ before the thematic vowel.
The Greek reflex must have undergone dissimilation.

The vocalism in Latin has widely been considered troublesome and is usually explained away as an old s-stem. §Höfler0§, however, posits an additional unknown laryngeal between _*m_ and _*s_ which, with a nominative singular o-grade, would not surface due to Saussure's Law. In the e-grade of the dual, however, it would, which is where the Latin form comes from. This view is adopted in this dictionary entry. For more information, please consult the source.

§Beekes1§ reconstructs the Proto-Germanic etymon with _*-ī-_ although §Kroonen3§ disagrees. While the _*l~*n_ alteration may date back to Proto-Indo-European times, it is more likely we are dealing with two separate derivations, a view which is supported by the difference in length. While the Germanic form may be traced back to the diminutive suffix _*-ilaz_, either Hoffmann's suffix _*-hₓn-_ or the derivational _*-ihₓnos_ may be identified in the Graeco-Armeno-Carite derivation. The presence of an o-grade in Armenian as well as its classification as an a-stem points towards an independent Armenian derivation, while it is impossible to point out if the Graeco-Carite derivations, which are formally identical, are independent or areal innovations. While the association between hedgehogs and snakes appears to be common and a linguistic analysis of hedgehog as “snake-eater” checks out zoologically, an actual derivation only makes sense phonologically in Greek as its word for snake, grc@ἔχις=ékhis, would be the only pure reflex of a hypothetical pie@h₁éǵʰis, being displaced by pie@@h₃égʷʰis in other branches. Any corruption of reflexes of the latter or of the lexeme for hedgehog in descendants must thus be secondary.

This word appears to have been reshaped significantly in the different branches, presumably due to taboo. The Balto-Slavic mobile accent contrasts with what we find in other branches and may be due to analogy with the feminine form.
The thematicisation into a masculine o-stem is common to all post-Anatolian languages, and must predate the Carite vocalisation of consonant stems into i-stems.
pslv@ostrovъ would be identical, if not for the prefix.
As evidenced by got@𐍅𐌴𐌹𐌷𐍃=weihs, the Germanic branch also contained a reflex; however, neither §Kroonen3§ nor §Ringe0§ mention the exact Proto-Germanic form.

meaning: pagan god of archery and solar chariot
vcb.etymoprose: In the Carite pantheon, this god continues one of the divine horse twins alongside °HORSETWIN2°, more specifically the young warrior, and his depiction varies from a young man riding a horse to a centaur. Functional equivalents include the grc@Διόσκοροι=Dióskoroi. Onomastically, this deity is a derivation of the common word for horse, pie@h₁éḱwos (cf. °EKWOS°).

The Greek verb is most likely a denominative of an unattested *κοῖμος (_*koîmos_), which would be formally identical to the Germano-Carite nouns. §Beekes1§ mentions a cognate in pslv@sěmьja which appears to be missing from §Derksen0§.

§Beekes1§ mentions that the word may actually be substrate in origin. The secondary meaning of female genitalia, which is also present in the Greek reflex, eventually overtook the animal meaning in Carite.
The original Anlaut, presumably _*pst-_, is widely debated due to the variety in which it appears in different daughter languages.

The large amount of discrepancies may point towards a substrate origin, as is common for bird names. grc@ψάρ=psár is probably unrelated according to §Beekes1§, but was included in this dictionary anyway.

The Armeno-Celtic cognates are derivations of the feminine equivalent, with the Celtic reflex being a derivation using _*-Vnos_ (often used to indicate possession) and the Armenian reflex being a compound with hye@@ayr ("man"). In Slavic, the consonant was altered through analogy with the feminine equivalent.

The form _*h₂entíos_ is labelled as Post-Proto-Indo-European by §Ringe0§. Despite not having had any contact with the Germanic people until the time of the Visigoths, we may find the same accentuation in Greek, which is likely a development shared by Carite.
The presence of an unvoiced dental plosive in Latin can easily be explained through analogy. For a more in-depth explanation, see§de Vaan1§.
pgmc@westeraz may belong here, but this is still rather uncertain.

While the Proto-Celtic voicing of _*pr_ to _*br_ is regular, the initial _*g_ is unusual. §Matasović3§ posits assimilation with the following _*b_ or contamination with pie@gʰayd-, which is not attested in Celtic and furthermore considered to be a loan (cf. °GHAYD°). §de Vaan1§ instead suggests that the voicing discrepancy is the result of _*kápros_ being a loan itself, a claim the phonemic _*a_ may confirm. §Mallory2§ suggests a derivation from pie@kápr̥ “penis”, which is no less problematic.
The numerous alterations in the cognates can be ascribed to tabooistic distortion.

§de Vaan1§ compares the reflexes to grc@ἄρκευθος=árkeuthos and pslv@orkỳta and assumes a substrate word. However, the presence of the labialisation in Germano-Celtic while it is missing from Greek is problematic.

meaning: pagan god of medicine and lunar chariot
vcb.etymoprose: In the Carite pantheon, this god continues one of the divine horse twins alongside °HORSETWIN2°, more specifically the young warrior, and his depiction varies from a young man riding a horse to a centaur. Functional equivalents include the grc@Διόσκοροι=Dióskoroi.
pgmc@gudą ("god") may be a cognate as well.
hye@ուստր=ustr, mentioned as a cognate by §Mallory2§, is derived from a different root by §Martirosyan0§. §de Vaan1§ mentions pslv@pъtákъ as cognate, to which §Derksen0§ assigns no etymology.
§Beekes1§ mentions a formally identical rus@plov, of which no further trace can be found.
Unlike most other sources, §Matasović3§ claims that the Celtic form derives from a zero grade formation rather than an o-grade. This vision is adopted in this dictionary.
An old agent noun unique to Carite of Indo-European age related to °WERGOMWORK°.

A noun without any formal correspondences in other languages. The Proto-Indo-European formation most likely meant "breather" and the semantic shift of such word to animal is widely attested, with examples including lat@animal and pgmc@deuzą (but note that pclt@dwosyos, its cognate, refers to humans instead). Please refer to °PNEWMI° for further etymology and sources.
The Germanic cognate only differs in stress.

§Ringe0§ reconstructs the Germanic reflex as _*nistaz_, which would be the expected result. However, as shown by §Kroonen3§, all Germanic languages show a neuter gender, which means it's more than likely it was already neuter at Proto-Germanic times. The origin of the velar in the Slavic etymon is unknown and postdates the Balto-Slavic split.
sqi@shok, while related, was borrowed from the Latin cognate.

Given the feminine gender of the Germano-Slavic reflexes, §Beekes1§ mentions that the word may have been an old feminine, although he says the shift in gender would be unusual. Additionally, the neuter gender of the Sanskrit reflex doesn't clear up anything. Perhaps the feminine reflexes are old collectives? Anyhow, the Carite form perfectly mirrors the Greek reflex.

§Beekes1§ explains the variation in vowel length in Greek as the result of laryngeal metathesis, i.e. _*phₓurós_. If the short vowel is the result of pretonic shortening, i.e. Dybo's law, however, grc@πυρός=purós is also formally identical to the Carite reflex. Despite the ability to reconstruct a Proto-Indo-European form, this word may be an old Wanderwort instead. ang@fyrs is also mentioned, but no Proto-Germanic form can be found.

meaning: mythological realm of the Chthonic deities

vcb.etymoprose: §Matasović3§ explains the voiceless velar in Celtic by assimilation from an original _*-s_ (see also °HORTUS°).
§Mallory2§ reconstructs the root as pie@@h₁reyhₓ- instead.
For the presence of _*h₂_ in the Carite forms, see °HORN°.

A word with a slightly troublesome etymology. While the a-vocalism in Latin can easily be explained (see §de Vaan1§), the Greek form is slightly more problematic. While §de Vaan1§ vouches for a zero grade with analogy to the verb, the Mycenaean attestation lacks the rhotic. §Beekes1§ suggests a non-Indo-European origin instead, which §de Vaan1§ finds unlikely given the presence of a Latino-Balto-Slavic verb. In any case, Carite shows the regular outcome of a zero grade.

§Beekes1§ points out that lat@sūcus (whence °SUCUS°), while similar, is clearly deviant. However, as §de Vaan1§ notes, we find both _*suḱ-_ and _*sug-_ as zero grades, which only complicates it even further. If we posit an o-grade _*souk-_ and assume an early metathesis into _*sokw-~sokʷ-_, we may reconcile the two forms. However, the variation in velar remains problematic. This vacillation may be explained by looking for a non-Indo-European origin, such as purl@śuwe.
The Greek lengthening appears to be secondary. §Martirosyan0§ posits a related hye@Գէն=Gēn which would be formally identical to lat@vēna, which §de Vaan1§ does not mention.
The a-vocalism in the Greek reflex is irregular. §Beekes1§ suggests a possible intermediate language it was loaned from. The Armenian cognate is not mentioned by §Martirosyan0§.

The stressed zero grade in Germanic, as proven by the absence of Verner's Law, is clearly deviant when compared to the Greek and Sanskrit forms. In Latin, Slavic and Celtic, the _*-wós_ suffix from pie@gʷih₃wós (whence °VIVUS°) contaminated the original formation to different degrees. The semantic shift from “mortal” to “human” is extremely common, with there being a perfect parallel in hye@մարդ=mard as well as similar shifts in other words such as lat@mortālis and grc@βρότειος=bróteios.
The vocalisation of _*l̥_ in the Greek cognate may point towards a late thematicisation.
A very old epithet that appears to be a compound of the words that yield °NERO° and °GWHENMI°, meaning “man-slayer”. The Greek cognate is notoriously close but they may be independent formations.
The reconstruction _*ses(y)ós_, which §Mallory2§ posits, leaves the Celtic vowel unexplained and is thus untenable.

meaning: he who can not be woken

vcb.etymoprose: While both §Mallory2§ and §Martirosyan0§ include a Celtic cognate in sga@erc (“heaven”), the word is noteworthily missing from §Matasović3§. §Martirosyan0§ also mentions the Irish word for heaven being a reflex of the god of thunder, for which see °PERKUNAS°.
We may be dealing with a Mediterranean word per §Martirosyan0§.
The reconstruction _*pr̥h₃ḱtós_ posited by §Mallory2§ is untenable.
A word of dubious origin. The most popular etymology is a derivation of pie@med-, shifting in meaning from “he who is measured” to “he who is judged” and finally to “criminal”.

The labiovelar is sometimes reconstructed as aspirated to account for the Celtic reflex; however, this would be incompatible with the Slavic and Greek reflexes. See §Matasović3§ for a more in-depth explanation on how pclt@owignos may have come into being.
From the original paradigm _*h₂nēr_ ($acc _*h₂nérm̥_, $gen _*h₂n̥rós_), Carite appears to have thematicised the genitive stem whereas Celtic generalised the accusative stem.
§Matasović3§ reconstructs the root as pie@@ḱewh₂- instead, but _*h₁_ would share its reflex with _*h₂_ in this environment anyway.
Presumably a loanword from a common European source, as also hinted at by the similarity between different bird names in Greek.

§Derksen0§ and §de Vaan1§ prefer to reconstruct pie@@*gleh₁y- as the root, but this would not have a difference in the Carite outcome. §Matasović3§ posits pie@@gleyhₓ- instead, which would require Dybo's law for the Proto-Celtic verb pclt@@glināti. §Martirosyan0§ posits an additional pie@@gl̥yeh₂-, which is problematic for multiple reasons. Either way, the exact reconstruction is uncertain. The original suffix of the Greek reflex is uncertain; if _*-yos_, it is formally identical to the Germanic reflex instead.

The Latin outcome is irregular and may be through folk etymology, possibly through analogy with lat@vīvus? Balto-Slavic cognates are mentioned in multiple sources but seemingly missing from §Derksen0§; they are mentioned in §Derksen1§, however. §Kroonen3§ attempts to connect the seemingly unrelated Germanic reflex by including a laryngeal, yielding the root pie@@h₂wer-. However, this would also surface in the reduplications as _*h₂ey-_, _*h₂wi-_, _*h₂i-_ and even _*h₂oy-_, making this a very ad hoc solution. His explanation, being that the daughters independently restored the reduplication after the loss of laryngeals, is unconvincing. As suggested by §Mallory2§ among others, by analysing the Germanic formation as a compound of the word for “oak”, pgmc@aiks, and the Proto-Indo-European root pie@@wer- reconstructed by the other scholars, we may solve the puzzle without any new issues emerging.

Rather than _*-eh₃i-_, we may also be dealing with _*-ohₓi-_. The discrepancy between _*-m-_ and _*-n-_ in the descendants may stem from an original _*-mn-_ and/or from dissimilation of _*-m-_ due to the preceding labial plosive. §Derksen1§ suggests a connection to pie@speh₁-, which would have meant “to be filled to the rim” rather than “to succeed”.
§Kroonen3§ mentions this root also probably surfaces in hye@թեղաւշ=tʿeławš, where it would be the second member of the compound. §Martirosyan0§, however, does not mention this at all.

meaning: pagan goddess of love and fertility
pagan goddess of life and day
vcb.etymoprose: §Beekes1§ also connects pclt@wāri- (“sunrise, east”) through _*h₂wōsri-_. §Matasović3§, however, prefers pie@wesr̥. While the meaning strongly correlates to pie@@h₂ews-, the lengthened o-grade through Schwebeablaut feels rather far-fetched.

According to §Beekes1§, the connection to the Greek reflex is tentative at best because of apparent remodeling after grc@ὀξύς=oxús (which is also possibly non-Indo-European) and the presence of the Pre-Greek suffix -ιν-. Furthermore, §Kroonen3§ vouches for a European origin instead. The actual Latin development into _-cc-_ is unclear; §de Vaan1§ offers several convincing explanations. §Mallory2§ reconstructs a new root _*{h₁,h₂}ek-_, possibly with a regular velar to explain the presence of /k/ in the Baltic forms; §Derksen0§ and §Derksen1§ explain this deviation as a borrowing from Germanic instead, vouching for the semantic distance between the Slavic and Balto-Germanic words. As it is preferable to retain the connection to pie@h₂eḱ- (“sharp”) or to simply consider it to be of non-Indo-European origin, the reconstruction of a separate root is unnecessary.
The formation is a variation on pie@udéros, for which see °UTERUS°.
The semantic shift in Carite appears to be similar to the shift in Germanic, but is almost certainly an independent development.
The connection to the non-Celtic reflexes is uncertain.
While the status of the root is unsure, the Carite forms seem to mirror the Greek one perfectly. §Matasović3§ categorises cym@erw under pie@h₂erh₃- instead.
Probably of substrate origin.
The two Celtic terms were in fact distinct.

The Proto-Indo-European formation is most likely Post-Proto-Indo-European, being restricted to Italo-Germano-Carite. §Kroonen3§ suggests for a formal variant of pie@h₂eP- over a loan from a non-Indo-European language. §Kilday0§ makes an interesting case for the root pie@@h₁eh₁kʷ-, whence the root-accent zero grade formation pie@@h₁h̥́₁kʷeh₂. This formation is incompatible with the Carite reflex, however. For more information, please consult the source.

The actual reconstruction of the root differs between authors, with the middle laryngeal being reconstructed both as _*h₁_ and _*h₂_. While this is irrelevant to the outcome in Carite, _*h₂_ seems more likely due to the Doric variant λᾶνος (_lânos_), if not a hyperdorism. More prevalent is the reconstruction with with an initial _*h₂-_. This laryngeal is reconstructed on the basis of the initial _ḫ-_ in Hittite. §Matasović3§ ascribes this to metathesis however, as neither Greek form shows any trace of the expected word-initial α- (_a-_). While §Beekes1§ says the laryngeal might have been there originally, it must have vanished disappeared early in Greek history, possibly through dissimilation. The presence of the laryngeal would not affect the Carite outcome as Engels' law would require _*h₂w-_ to be followed by a vowel. As pointed out by §Kroonen3§, the Germanic reflex requires a suffix-stressed form which slightly deviates from the others; however, §Ringe0§ departs from a radically stressed form instead.

It is not clear if the shift from “heel” to “weakness” was influenced the myth of Achilles, but the similarity is too striking to be a mere coincidence. The underlying root is sometimes thought to be related to °HEEL2°.
The Armenian cognate is slightly problematic and may not be related after all.

The actual form of this root is not entirely clear. §Matasović3§ reconstructs an unknown root-final laryngeal and posits a zero grade formation to account for the long vowel; the full grade would result into _**reimā_. However, as he points out, this extra laryngeal is not reflected in Greek. §Kroonen3§ considers _*h₂rey-_ to be a reanalysis of _*h₂rh₁ey-_, an i-present to pie@@h₂reh₁-. In Germano-Carite, both _*-ihₓ-_ and _*-ey(hₓ)-_ result in _*-ī-_, so the precise reconstruction is irrelevant for these branches.
The underlying root is sometimes thought to be related to °HEEL1°.
If an initial laryngeal is reconstructed, its identity is not agreed upon. Nonetheless, the presence of the initial φ- (_f-_) in Carite points towards an original word-initial laryngeal.
lit@kiškà may be related as well.

Often reconstructed as _*dʰólh₂os_ - however, the only thing pointing towards a laryngeal would be the inclusion of grc@θαλάμη=thalámē, which §Beekes1§ refutes. Likewise, the inclusion of grc@θόλος=thólos per §Mallory2§ should be discarded.

The different reflexes showcase a wide variety of unexpected alterations and reconstructing a single root or form is difficult. Either way, the Carite form seems to perfectly mirror the Celtic form, including the reformed full grade without the laryngeal. For a more in-depth explanation, see §Matasović3§. Slavic cognates are not mentioned by §Derksen0§.
The Carite formation appears to be a thematicisation of the original collective.
§Beekes1§ considers the appurtenance of the Latin and Albanian cognates to be doubtful because of the unexpected reflex of the first stop.

§Martirosyan0§ does not include the Celtic cognate and, on account of the missing prosthetic vowel in Armenian, posits a Mediterranean substrate origin instead. Additionally, since the Armeno-Greek forms imply _*srungʰ-_, their reflexes are hard to reconcile. It is likely that the root was originally onomatopoeic and later independent onomatopoeic alterations are responsible for the vascillation.
It is likely a similar diminutive existed in Celtic.
The Celtic form may be from an original o-grade instead.
Transparently an old derivation of °ASTER°.

Probably of substrate origin. The meaning of “danewort” as opposed to other trees, as is the case in e.g. Slavic, is restricted to Italo-Carite. The Gaulish gal@odocos is often connected, but §Delamarre0§ connects it to pie@h₃ed- "to smell" instead. The connection to grc@ἐλάτη=elátē as posited by §Friedrich0§ must be discarded.
The Greek cognate would be formally identical if not for the suffixal vowel of unknown origin. Some sources construct a palatovelar instead, which would be irrelevant to the Carite outcome.
The Anlaut fricative in Latin is problematic.
A formation that appears to be unique to Carite.
§Ringe0§ vouches for a pie@@landʰom origin of pgmc@landą, of which §Kroonen3§ disapproves.
Most likely of onomatopoeic origin. A Slavic cognate appears to be missing from §Derksen0§.
A tree name of North-Western substrate origin.
While the initial laryngeal is not always reconstructed, it is required for the Carite onset. The Albanian reflex may be a Latin loan.

meaning: meat used as food for pets
pagan goddess of earth and agriculture

vcb.etymoprose: §Beekes1§ argues that grc@μάλθη=málthē, which §Mallory2§ posits as cognate, is a Pre-Greek technical loan and thus unrelated. The Germanic cognate is not mentioned in §Kroonen3§ or §Ringe0§.
The reconstruction pie@pólh₂m̥ posited by §Mallory2§ is untenable.

§Beekes1§'s assumption that the word is Pre-Greek is refuted by §Nikolaev4§, who proposes a plausible etymology that allows connection to Indo-Iranian cognates, as well as a perfect match to the Carite term for afterlife.
Of onomatopoeic origin.
The Germanic cognates are mentioned by §Matasović3§ but are missing in §Kroonen3§ and §Ringe0§. Almost undoubtedly of substrate origin.
This word was most likely feminine in Proto-Indo-European, with the noun class changing accordingly in Carite. The Germanic form is only formally identical without the _*j_.
Only §Hyllested0§ vouches for the connection between all etymons.
The Slavic forms are problematic as the expected vowel colouring does not occur.

meaning: pagan goddess of the moon, healing and the sea
pagan god of cattle, music and art
pagan god of the sky and rain
